p:QAT: The Qatar Central Bank issues the riyal (QAR), held at a fixed rate to the US dollar (a peg). Its law scores 0.607 of 1 on one independence index and 0.586 on another, where 1 means the bank holds the power. Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters in 2010-2018, and no documented case at the bank was found. Where the bank sits is set out in its own law and has no end date. Under Law No. 13 of 2012, issued by the Emir, the bank is a corporate body with its own capital and budget and is under the direct control of the Emir; the Governor is appointed by Emiri decision for a renewable five-year term with the rank of a minister, and the board seats representatives of the ministries responsible for finance and for trade. It has 4 swap lines, which are agreements to borrow another central bank's currency. They include CNY 35 billion with China, with a renewal agreement dated 14 October 2026, and USD 15 billion equivalent in lira and riyal with Türkiye, amended in 2020, whose current status is not confirmed. It holds 116.2 tonnes of gold, 26.8% of reserves. The exposure score is 29 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 fully exposed. De La Rue printed the 22-riyal commemorative note issued for the 2022 FIFA World Cup.
p:SAU: Saudi Arabia's money is the riyal, issued by the Saudi Central Bank and held at a fixed rate against the United States dollar. It scores 30 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. The independence the law gives it is thinner: 0.501 of 1 on an index of 42 rules, rank 138 of 155, where 1 would mean the bank rather than the government holds the power, and 0 on the part covering control of its own money and budget. It tells the public little, 5.5 of 15 on a transparency measure, and no case at the bank is documented, which is not proof that none happened. The arrangement that matters here is in the law. Under the Saudi Central Bank Law, issued by Royal Decree M/36 of 26 November 2020 and shown as in force on the bank's own rulebook, the bank reports to the King; its five non-government board members are nominated jointly by the Governor and the Minister of Finance and appointed by royal order, and their pay is set by royal order on the Minister of Finance's recommendation. The rulebook's own footnotes record the Council of Ministers amending one of its articles by resolution. The bank part-owns the Bank for International Settlements, the bank for central banks in Basel; its officials also sit on the Financial Stability Board, and it holds 323.1 tonnes of gold. It has one swap line, an arrangement to borrow another central bank's currency, signed with China on 20 November 2023 for three years and worth 50 billion yuan or 26 billion riyals. Governor Fahad Al-Mubarak came from private finance: general manager of Rana Investment Company from 1992 to 1999, then chairman and managing director of Morgan Stanley Saudi Arabia. He was governor from 2011 to 2016, and King Salman named him governor again by royal decree on 24 January 2021; no ethics finding is recorded against him. Banknotes are reported to be printed at home by the Saudi Central Bank Printing Works. PricewaterhouseCoopers and Ernst & Young Professional Services audited the accounts for the year ended 30 June 2023.
p:SGP: The Monetary Authority of Singapore is the central bank that issues the Singapore dollar. It scores 24 of 100 for outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed, making it less exposed than 88% of 194 places scored; its weakest side is that the country's laws hide who owns money. No documented case was found. Who chairs it is a matter of record, and it is the cabinet: the Authority announced that from 8 July 2023 the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance would chair its Board of Directors, with the Minister for Trade and Industry as Deputy Chairman, succeeding a chairman who had held the post for twelve years while serving as a Senior Minister. The arrangement continues; the Authority's own board page now lists the Chairman as the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry and the Deputy Chairman as the Minister for National Development, with a Minister of State and the Attorney-General also on the board. Under a 1967 agreement, Brunei and Singapore accept each other's notes and coins at par. The bank is part-owner of the Bank for International Settlements, which 63 central banks own, and belongs to the Financial Stability Board. Former chairman Tharman Shanmugaratnam is a member of the Group of Thirty. It has 16 swap lines (agreements to borrow another central bank's currency). Note Printing Australia prints its banknotes. Ong Chong Tee, a Deputy Managing Director of the authority, was appointed a director of the commercial United Overseas Bank on 1 January 2023 and chairs its audit committee; he is also a director of AIA Group.
p:CRI: The Central Bank of Costa Rica issues the country's money and, as of December 2025, keeps it within a moving band of plus or minus 2 percent against the US dollar. It scores 23 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence; outside influence alone scores 5, and the weak side is corruption and secrecy around the bank, at 52. Its notes are printed abroad: an international tender was opened in the second half of 2008 among the makers on the bank's supplier register for six new denominations, and Oberthur won it, with the 20,000-colon note of 2010 recorded as printed by Oberthur Technologies on cotton fibre paper at its plant in Rennes. That rests on Spanish Wikipedia and a numismatic blog rather than on a document from the bank. The independence written into its law is high, 0.826 of 1 on one index. Government pressure was reported in 1 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, and that instance was a threat to change the law. A later episode is on record: in January 2024 three serving cabinet ministers, for foreign trade, agriculture and tourism, each wrote to the bank's president demanding a revision of exchange-rate policy, and the President backed the approach at a press conference. No documented case at the bank was found, which does not prove none happened. Semanario Universidad reports that the bank hired BlackRock in 2017 as a co-administrator of its international reserves and that BlackRock holds 5.5 percent of them, about 352 million US dollars, the bank telling the paper that hiring outside portfolio managers is usual practice in central banking. The Contraloria General de la Republica audits the accounts under the 1995 central bank law, which is in force. Rodrigo Cubero became president of the bank in 2018; La Republica reported on 6 August 2018, as he took over, that he had worked several years at the International Monetary Fund, most recently as deputy division chief at the IMF's Institute for Capacity Development, and that he had not taken part in the IMF reports that had advised the bank.
p:MDV: The Maldives Monetary Authority issues the Maldivian rufiyaa, and its record turns on one scandal: the embezzlement of 1.3 billion rufiyaa from the Maldives Marketing and Public Relations Corporation. An Anti-Corruption Commission report made public in February 2019 found the authority negligent. Its Financial Intelligence Unit, the office that watches for suspicious money, was told in 2014 of a 59 million US dollar cheque from that company to a firm called SOF but did not look into it properly, did not examine SOF's large transactions through the Bank of Maldives and the Bank of Ceylon, and did not pass suspected money-laundering cases on. The unit's former head, Ibrahim Athif Shakoor, said governor Azeema Adam objected to filing a police report, citing too few staff and resources; Azeema said she had told him to investigate SOF's transactions and gave no specific instructions because the unit decided its own actions. In March 2019 police summoned governor Ahmed Naseer and confirmed he was being investigated for obstruction of justice, with no charge or court outcome named. He resigned in July 2019 amid allegations that he had got around the authority's rules and interfered in the unit's inquiries, one of them into a 22.5 million rufiyaa deposit to then-President Abdulla Yameen's account shortly before the 2018 election; Naseer denied influencing the unit and made counter-allegations, and no charges or findings followed. In February 2020 the Prosecutor General's Office charged Shakoor with negligence and failing to act appropriately on the case; he denied the allegations, and on 14 October 2025 that office withdrew the charge, citing how long it had been in court, with no conviction reported. One career move is documented: Ali Hashim, who was finance minister under former president Mohamed Nasheed from November 2008 to December 2010 and who also chaired the Addu International Airport Company during the previous MDP government, with no years given for that, was nominated by President Ibrahim Mohamed Solih for the vacant post of governor of the authority, as reported on 29 August 2019. Deloitte Partners in Male' audited the 2024 accounts. On 7 October 2024 India agreed a currency-borrowing line of 400 million US dollars and 30 billion Indian rupees. The authority scores 38 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Its notes are printed abroad. De La Rue's launch release says the family of six notes introduced on 1 November 2015, from 10 to 1,000 rufiyaa, was designed by local designer Abdullah Nashaath and printed by De La Rue on polymer, in close association with the Monetary Authority. Parliament has also opened the bank's own balance sheet to the government. On 23 November 2021 the People's Majlis approved the Finance Ministry's request to extend to the end of 2023 the overdraft of the public account at the Monetary Authority, by 42 votes; it had earlier suspended parts of the Fiscal Responsibility Act to allow 4.4 billion rufiyaa to be overdrawn, of which 2.5 billion was converted into a fifty-year amortising bond held by the Authority at 2.5 per cent.
p:BIH: The convertible mark is issued by the Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina under a currency board: marks are put into circulation only against convertible foreign currency the bank holds, at 1.95583 marks to the euro, and its monetary liabilities may never exceed its foreign currency assets. It is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, and it has joined the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, which offers advice, training and asset management, with the announcement stating the membership rather than which of those services the bank takes. Its law scores 0.899 of 1 for independence, 11th of 155 countries, and no government pressure was reported in the quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case is documented: in 2023 a criminal complaint accused governor Senad Softic of suspected wrongdoing in several matters, including a project to acquire an office building in Pale and a procedure to buy land in Sarajevo. The prosecutor's office said in February 2023 that it had opened a case and was verifying the allegations, which remain unproven, while the bank said examining allegations is not an investigation and that reports of one were untrue. Grant Thornton d.o.o. Banja Luka audited the 2016 accounts. The state has twice acted on the bank. On 25 June 2019 two of the five members of its Governing Board were dismissed by the country's tripartite Presidency, with the reasons unclear. And in April 2025 the Council of Ministers adopted a revised state budget that settled an arbitration liability out of the bank's profits; the bank suspended the transfer of 244.3 million marks, part of its 412.6 million marks of 2024 net profit, to the Ministry of Finance and Treasury, saying the move endangered its assets. The bank holds 3.5 tonnes of gold and scores 39 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. One career move is recorded. The Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina's own profile page gives Jasmina Selimovic's dated career: at the Faculty of Economics in Sarajevo since 2004, its Dean from 2018 and renewed in 2022; in the Fiscal Council's advisory group from 2011 to 2015; an independent member of the Supervisory Board of Raiffeisen Bank Bosnia and Herzegovina in 2018; president of the board of the Sarajevo Canton Institute of Health Insurance since 2021; and a member of the bank's Governing Board from 3 January 2024. The central bank's page leaves the ownership of Raiffeisen Bank Bosnia and Herzegovina unstated; that bank's own ownership page lists Raiffeisen SEE Region Holding GmbH as sole owner at 100 per cent, with no state shareholder, which is what makes this a move involving a private bank. Moving between jobs is not wrongdoing.
p:GUY: The Bank of Guyana issues the Guyanese dollar, held at what is in practice a fixed rate to the US dollar as of December 2025. It scores 31 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 fully exposed, and the weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, at 56, with the country scoring 40 of 100 on the Corruption Perceptions Index. Independence written into its law scores 0.609 of 1, ranking 93 of 191, and no government pressure was reported in 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. No case at the bank is recorded, which is not proof none happened. Two career moves are on record. The first is entirely within the public sector, so it is listed but not counted: governor Gobind Ganga directed the bank's research department from 1995 to November 2003, left to be an alternate executive director at the World Bank in Washington, returned as deputy governor in June 2005 and became governor on 2 December 2014. No private employer appears anywhere in the career the bank publishes. Crane Currency is listed as having supplied banknotes, banknote paper and anti-counterfeiting features, though that comes from a client list in another body's announcement rather than a contract notice. The second runs the other way and into private banking: Demerara Bank, which its own audited accounts describe as incorporated in January 1992 as a private limited liability company, publishes a profile of its director Rajendra Rampersaud saying he has more than two decades of central banking experience and served as a Director at the Bank of Guyana until 2018. The Auditor General audits the accounts.
p:COL: The Bank of the Republic issues Colombia's peso and prints it at its own banknote works; it is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the bank used by central banks themselves. One case is recorded: in 2011 two officials were investigated for allegedly passing reserved information about people and companies to the DAS security agency and were suspended for a month, but in January 2011 the bank reported that the Procuraduria's ruling on appeal revoked the suspension, finding they had broken no rule. Government pressure was reported in 2 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, each time to cut rates. On 31 July 2025, after the board voted 4 to 3 to hold the rate at 9.25 per cent, President Gustavo Petro accused the bank of wanting to “finish off the economy” and of having an electoral bet. Amundi won a mandate in 2023, as one of eight outside managers, over 1.7 billion US dollars of its assets, and its reserve gold sits in the custody of the Bank of England, which is storage rather than management. Leonardo Villar became general manager in January 2021 after serving as an executive director at the International Monetary Fund. A second career runs out of the bank into private banking: Gerardo Hernandez Correa spent sixteen years at the Bank of the Republic, as a board member, executive manager and secretary of the board, then six years as the country's financial superintendent, then from 2021 vice-president for legal affairs at Banco de Bogota, and in June 2024 was named president of Banco AV Villas. Both are commercial banks in which Grupo Aval, a private conglomerate, holds controlling stakes.
p:MDA: The National Bank of Moldova issues the leu, which is held within 2 percent of the euro. Its law scores 0.861 of 1 for independence, where 1 means the bank holds the power, and it scores 30 of 100 for exposure to outside influence. Dorin Dragutanu resigned as governor on 21 September 2015 after criticism for failing to prevent about 1 billion dollars disappearing from three Moldovan banks; he blamed pressure from politicians and denied responsibility, and President Nicolae Timofti and Prime Minister Valeriu Strelet had both said he should go. On 5 March 2020 prosecutors searched the bank's headquarters and detained deputy governor Cincilei, former deputy governor Tabirta and a division head on suspicion of fraud and money laundering tied to that theft, which surfaced in 2014 and 2015 after the bank made a 13 billion leu emergency loan later turned into public debt; they also moved to arrest Dragutanu. None of it is proven. On the evening of 21 December parliament dismissed governor Octavian Armasu by 81 votes, citing insufficient and defective work on the fraud case. KPMG Moldova SRL checks the bank's accounts from outside. Armasu had come to the bank from the government: he became Governor on 30 November 2018, appointed for a seven-year term, having served before that as Moldova's Minister of Finance. A second career runs in from the auditors rather than from a bank. The bank's own biography of Constantin Schendra, appointed Deputy Governor by a parliamentary decision of 4 November 2021, records more than eight years in international audit companies: senior auditor at Ernst & Young Moldova from 2010 to 2015 and at Ernst & Young Cyprus, then Baker Tilly Moldova, before joining the bank as director of banking supervision in 2018. Those are private firms in professional services rather than banks or insurers.
p:GEO: The National Bank of Georgia issues the lari. Its law scores 0.847 of 1 for independence from government, and it scores 26 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. On 17 July 2015 parliament voted 80 to 19 to move banking supervision out of the bank to a new agency, after Bidzina Ivanishvili blamed the bank and its chairman Giorgi Kadagidze for the lari's fall. In September 2023 the bank unfroze assets tied to Otar Partskhaladze, a former Prosecutor General sanctioned by the US Treasury, arguing that Georgian citizens cannot be sanctioned without a conviction in a Georgian court; acting president Natia Turnava confirmed on 20 September that she had changed the procedure single-handedly, three of the four vice presidents and an adviser resigned, and no court verdict or official finding followed. In 2026 the Prosecutor's Office began investigating Council member Nana Keinishvili over possible unlawful involvement in business, after complaints from the crypto firm Bitexchange LLC, which the bank had fined; it was still open in October 2026 and nothing is proven. The World Bank's Reserves Advisory and Management Partnership advises the bank on its reserves investment strategy and gold policy rather than managing the money. KPMG Georgia LLC audited the bank's accounts for 2020, signing at Tbilisi on 23 April 2021. Koba Gvenetadze was picked as president by the bank's board on 16 March 2016 and approved by the President of Georgia the next day, replacing Giorgi Kadagidze; he had joined the International Monetary Fund in 2002 and was its resident representative in Azerbaijan from early 2008 to late 2009 and in Kyrgyzstan from 2010 to 2014, and he was Georgia's Deputy Finance Minister in 2000 and 2001. One career runs in from a commercial bank. The bank's own profile of Vice-Governor Nino Jeladze, in post since 10 February 2025 for a term to February 2032, gives eighteen dated years at ProCredit: account manager at ProCredit Bank Georgia in 2003, head of customer service, branch manager including of the central branch from 2006 to 2014, operational risk manager, two years at ProCredit Holding in Frankfurt from 2015, and head of anti-money-laundering and compliance back in Georgia from 2017 to 2021. ProCredit Holding's own shareholder page names Zeitinger Invest, the German state development bank KfW, the DOEN foundation and the EBRD, so the ownership is mixed rather than plainly private.
p:NLD: The Netherlands uses the euro, whose rates the European Central Bank sets for the 21 countries on it, and De Nederlandsche Bank is the Dutch central bank inside that system; it scores 23 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. In June 2010 the Scheltema committee, set up by finance minister Wouter Bos, found that the bank had fallen seriously short in supervising DSB bank, missing flaws when licensing DSB in 2005 and being too patient afterwards, though it thought a different approach probably would not have prevented DSB's collapse. Parliament pressed the bank hard after that report: members called for a major overhaul of how it operates, the Christian Democrats said it had seriously fallen short as a regulator and that president Nout Wellink should explain publicly how he would restore its credibility, the GroenLinks member Jolande Sap said it would be very difficult to keep him on, and Roland van Vliet of the Freedom Party asked finance minister Jan Kees de Jager to sack him with a year of his term still to run. On 1 July 2010 the lower house voted on a motion of no confidence in Wellink and he survived it. He accepted the report's conclusions, which several members said was enough for them, and left at the end of his term in 2011. Two further findings sit at the European Central Bank: the European Ombudsman, the European Union's complaints office, found maladministration over president Mario Draghi's membership of the Group of Thirty, a forum of central bankers and private financiers, and in January 2018 recommended he suspend it, which the bank declined and he did not; and a board member's 18 May 2015 remarks in London that the bank would front-load asset purchases were published only the next morning, which the bank put down to an internal procedure error. Wim Duisenberg joined the Dutch bank in 1981 and became chairman in 1982, after three years at the International Monetary Fund and a seat on Rabobank's board. Most of its gold is stored for it rather than managed: 32 per cent at the Bank of England, 18.5 per cent at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and 18.5 per cent at the Royal Canadian Mint in Ottawa. EY Accountants B.V. audits the accounts for 2026 to 2032. The bank is unusually open about where its gold is. Its own website gives the split in plain words: 31 per cent, about 200,000 kilograms, at its own Cash Centre at Zeist, 32 per cent in the vaults of the Bank of England in London, 18.5 per cent at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and 18.5 per cent at the Royal Canadian Mint in Ottawa, out of more than 612 tonnes worth 72.2 billion euros at the end of 2025. Most central banks disclose nothing of the sort, or bury a single line in a note to the accounts.
p:MNG: The Bank of Mongolia issues the tugrik. Two cases and two departures centre on N. Zoljargal, governor from 2012, who was replaced on 20 July 2016, two years before his term was due to end and with no reason given. The anti-corruption agency IAAC arrested him on 29 November 2017 over the Chinggis bond and a price-stabilising programme, part of a wider look at how the bank was run from 2012 to 2016; a court released him with a travel ban, prosecutors had not formally charged him and no later outcome was found, so nothing there is proven. In April 2020 he and three politicians were reported charged with abuse of power over illegally transferring 49 per cent of the Erdenet Mining Company; no outcome is recorded and those charges are unproven too. Lawmakers accepted the resignation of his successor, Nadmid Bayartsaikhan, on 21 November 2019, after the Financial Action Task Force, which sets international rules against money laundering, put Mongolia on its grey list over enforcement. The present governor, B. Lkhagvasuren, came from the World Bank in Washington to the bank as adviser to the governor in 2000, and the rest of his career is in Mongolian public bodies. Two more careers run between the bank and the banks it supervises. Khosjargal Undraa joined the Supervisory Board in 2025 after thirteen years at Golomt Bank, from branch teller in 2006 to project director of its business process re-engineering project in 2018 and 2019, then deputy director of MIG LLC and chief executive of BPM Mongolia; Golomt's own account of itself says it was set up in 1995 as a subsidiary of Bodi International and became a joint-stock company at its 2022 listing, naming no state shareholder. Enkhjargal Danzanbaljir's career stays inside the public sector and so is listed without being counted: chief economist and adviser to the governor, London representative, Deputy Governor from 2007 to 2010, then the Asian Development Bank, the AIIB, the World Bank, an EU and GIZ project, the intergovernmental International Investment Bank and the state-owned State Bank of Mongolia, before rejoining the Supervisory Board in 2025. Ernst & Young Mongolia Audit LLC audited the accounts for the 2020 financial year, and Giesecke & Devrient printed the new 5,000-togrog note. It holds two currency swap lines with China, arrangements to lend each other money, one renewed on 26 June 2026 at 15 billion yuan against 7.85 trillion tugrik, and scores 31 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Where its gold is kept is disclosed, and the disclosure is going backwards. The bank's audited accounts for 2021 say its monetary gold and silver are mainly placed at the Bank of England and at JPMorgan Chase Bank, a commercial bank. The same note in the 2024 accounts drops both names and says only that the gold is held in foreign banks and in the vault of the Bank, so part of it is kept at home and the foreign holders are no longer named.
p:LBN: Banque du Liban issues Lebanon's currency, the Lebanese pound. Riad Salameh ran it for three decades until 2023, arriving from Merrill Lynch, where he worked from 1973 to 1993 and managed the personal portfolio of Rafic Hariri, the prime minister who then appointed him governor. A 2023 forensic audit by Alvarez & Marsal found the bank's foreign-currency position swung from a 7.2 billion US dollar surplus at the end of 2015 to a 50.7 billion dollar deficit at the end of 2020 with no loss shown on the balance sheet, and that Salameh set the accounting standards that concealed the losses and decided which banks benefited from financial engineering, unchallenged by the Central Council. The 2018 accounts, signed off with qualifications by EY and Deloitte, carried a 6.82 billion dollar asset called seigniorage on financial stability while the bank helped fund a widening government deficit. On 18 May 2020 the prosecutor Ali Ibrahim charged Mazen Hamdan, the bank's director of cash operations, with illegally manipulating the exchange rate; that charge is unproven. In May 2023 French prosecutors issued an arrest warrant for Salameh over illicit enrichment and alleged laundering of 330 million dollars, and Germany issued a second a week later; he called the French warrant a violation of the law. Arrested in Beirut in September 2024, held about thirteen months and released in September 2025 on bail of more than 14 million dollars, he was indicted with two lawyers in January 2026 over 44.8 million dollars allegedly taken from a consultancy account. He is also under investigation over allegations that more than 300 million dollars was siphoned off between 2002 and 2015 through Forry Associates, a company controlled by his brother Raja. All of it is unproven, and both brothers deny wrongdoing. The bank holds 286.8 tonnes of gold, 74.5 percent of its reserves, and scores 44 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Press reporting says KPMG was appointed in 2020 to audit the bank's accounts and that its findings have not been made public; this rests on a news report rather than a Banque du Liban document. Where the gold is kept is known only at second hand. The bank publishes no audited accounts, so the split rests on a 2026 policy paper from a research institute at the American University of Beirut, which says roughly two thirds of the holding sits in the bank's own vaults in Beirut and the rest at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The holding, about 287 tonnes, has not changed since 1971.
p:DZA: The Bank of Algeria issues the dinar and holds it within a band of 2 per cent or less against the euro. Algeria scores 43 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 87 per cent of the 194 places with a figure, its weakest side corruption and secrecy around the bank. Government pressure was reported in 3 of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, every time a demand to print money. One case is recorded, and it ended in acquittal: in the Khalifa Bank case the Blida criminal court sentenced former governor Abdelwahab Keramane in absentia to 20 years in prison in 2007, and on 7 June 2022 the same court acquitted him. On Monday 23 May 2022 Algeria's president Abdelmadjid Tebboune ended the duties of Rostom Fadhli as governor of the Bank of Algeria, with a statement from the presidency citing article 91 paragraph 7 and article 92 paragraph 7 of the constitution and giving no official reason; Fadhli had been appointed in June 2020 and had been expected to overhaul the 1990 money and credit law, a project that was not completed, and Salah Eddine Taleb, until then secretary of the Money and Credit Council, replaced him. The bank holds 173.6 tonnes of gold and is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Who checks its books is a state body rather than a firm, and the arrangement sits close to having no outside auditor at all. Under the money and credit law of 21 June 2023, a Censorat of two full-time censeurs, appointed by presidential decree and required to have central bank accounting expertise, verifies the end-of-year accounts, reports to the bank's board and sends a report to the Minister of Finance within four months of the year end. The censeurs are put there by the head of state rather than chosen by the bank, and they answer to a minister; but the Censorat is created by the bank's own charter law and its members sit in its board sessions, which is why this is recorded with the doubt attached. No private firm is named anywhere in the law for the bank's own accounts.
n:De Nederlandsche Bank Cash Centre, Zei: The Cash Centre at Zeist is De Nederlandsche Bank's own vault, and it holds the part of the country's gold that is kept at home: 31 per cent of the bank's holding, about 200,000 kilograms. The rest of the holding sits abroad with other institutions. A central bank that keeps gold in its own vault depends on nobody else to reach it, which is the whole point of the choice; the bank is also unusual in publishing the split by location in plain words rather than burying a single line in a note to its accounts.
n:JPMorgan Chase Bank: JPMorgan Chase Bank is a commercial bank. It appears here as a place where a central bank keeps gold: the Bank of Mongolia's audited accounts for 2021 say its monetary gold and silver are mainly placed at the Bank of England and at JPMorgan Chase Bank. That is worth noticing, because most gold custody on this map is held by other central banks or by a bank's own vaults, and a commercial bank holding a central bank's gold is a different kind of arrangement. Holding is not managing: a bank that keeps gold as a depository does not own it.
n:Bank of Mongolia's own vault, Ulaanbaa: This is the Bank of Mongolia's own vault. The bank's audited accounts for 2024 say its monetary gold is held in foreign banks and in the vault of the Bank, so part of the holding is kept at home. The same note no longer says which foreign banks, where earlier accounts named them, so the disclosure has gone backwards rather than forwards. A central bank that keeps gold in its own vault depends on nobody else to reach it.
n:Banque du Liban's own vaults, Beirut: The Banque du Liban keeps roughly two thirds of Lebanon's gold in its own vaults in Beirut, with the rest abroad. The holding, about 287 tonnes, has been unchanged since 1971 and is large for the size of the economy. None of this comes from the bank itself, which publishes no audited accounts: the split rests on a policy paper by a research institute at the American University of Beirut, and is marked as weakly sourced for that reason.
n:Censorat de la Banque d'Algerie: The Censorat is the body that checks the Bank of Algeria's books. It is not an accountancy firm. Under the money and credit law of 21 June 2023 it is made up of two full-time censeurs appointed by presidential decree, who must have central bank accounting expertise, who verify the end-of-year accounts and report to the bank's board, and who send a report to the Minister of Finance within four months of the year end. Calling that an audit from outside the bank is a fair question rather than a settled matter, and it is recorded here with the doubt attached: the Censorat is created by the bank's own charter law and its members sit in its board sessions, which is close to arrangements elsewhere that this map treats as having no external auditor at all. It is recorded because the censeurs are put in place by the head of state rather than chosen by the bank, and because they answer to a minister. No private firm is named anywhere in the law for the bank's own accounts.
